meta.title: What Counts as a Planet
meta.skill_frame: Find the main idea: decide what a whole passage is mostly about, not one true detail.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured FK 5.1-6.4 on the three parts, inside the grade 4-5 band. The load is the highest in the rung: the idea is about a definition and the argument around it, so the reader has to separate one famous case from the rule that produced it.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source._comment: Source: National Aeronautics and Space Administration, 'What is a planet?', https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/planets/what-is-a-planet/ (accessed 2026-10-28). U.S. federal government work, public domain in the U.S. Adapted for band 4: changes were made to the wording only.
source.basis: National Aeronautics and Space Administration, 'What is a planet?'.
source.attribution: National Aeronautics and Space Administration, 'What is a planet?', https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/planets/what-is-a-planet/, accessed 2026-10-28. U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
source.adaptation: Split long sentences, dropped the Greek and Copernican history, the quoted IAU resolution, and the exoplanet discussion, and kept the three-part rule and the Pluto case.
source.survey: The idea is about how a definition is made and argued over, which is harder than a fact about any one object.
source.avoided: No claim that the debate is settled. No number of dwarf planets the page only estimates.

session.difficulty_basis: Clue distance and how far the stated idea sits from the words the passage uses.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: The word planet comes from an old Greek word that means wanderer. For centuries, people used the word for the lights that moved across the sky. The meaning changed as people learned more. In 2006, a group of astronomers called the International Astronomical Union wrote a new definition. It said a planet must do three things. It must orbit a star. It must be big enough for gravity to pull it into a round shape. It must also have cleared other objects from its path. A dictionary defines a planet as any large body that circles the Sun. The word has changed meaning more than once.
passage.part_2: The new rule changed an old answer. Pluto was found in 1930 and was called the ninth planet. It is smaller than some of the planets' moons. In the 1990s, better telescopes found many icy objects beyond Neptune. They circle the Sun in a wide ring called the Kuiper Belt. Pluto is one of those objects. In 2005, astronomers found another object about the size of Pluto. People began to ask what a planet really is. Pluto had not cleared its path, so it became a dwarf planet. Ceres, found in 1801, was called a planet until more objects turned up in the same region.
passage.part_3: The vote did not end the argument. Some astronomers think the new rule was written to keep the list of planets short. Others think the rule is unclear. They ask how round an object must be, and how empty its path must be. Some would rather call any round object a planet. Others say a planet's place and makeup matter. Meanwhile, telescopes keep finding planets around other stars. The word planet may need another change. There may be billions of planets in the Milky Way, and some may be able to support life. Astronomers and planetary scientists still disagree about it.

items.prompt: What three things must a planet do?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. Orbit a star, be round from its own gravity, and clear its path.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The first part lists the three conditions of the 2006 definition.
tutor_only.tell: A planet must orbit a star, be round from gravity, and have cleared other objects from its path.
help: Count the conditions in the opening.
tutor_only.core_idea: A planet must orbit a star, be round from gravity, and have cleared its path.
accept_ideas: orbit a star, be round, and clear its path
circle a star, be round, and have an empty path
orbit, be round, and clear the area
not_required: the name of the group that voted

if_they_say.when: the student names only one or two conditions
if_they_say.ask: The passage lists three. Which one is missing?

items.prompt: Why did Pluto stop being called a planet?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. It shares its region with many icy objects, so it had not cleared its path.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The second part explains the Kuiper Belt, Pluto's place in it, and the third condition it fails.
tutor_only.tell: Pluto stopped being called a planet because it had not cleared other objects from its path.
help: Read the sentence about the Kuiper Belt.
The last sentence names the condition Pluto failed.
tutor_only.core_idea: Pluto had not cleared other objects from its path.
accept_ideas: it had not cleared its path
it shares its orbit with many icy objects
not_required: it is too far from the Sun

if_they_say.when: the student says Pluto is too small
if_they_say.ask: Small size is mentioned, but the rule that failed is about the path. What does the passage say about Pluto's path?

if_they_say.when: the student says astronomers lost interest in Pluto
if_they_say.ask: The change came from a rule. Which condition did Pluto fail?

items.prompt: What is this part mostly about?

tutor_only.confirm: Yes. The argument over the rule, which is not settled.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The part gives objections to the rule, competing ideas, and the note that the meaning may change again.
tutor_only.tell: This part is about the argument over the rule, which is still going on.
help: Look at what the astronomers disagree about.
The part ends with the meaning possibly changing again.
tutor_only.core_idea: The argument over the rule, which is still going on.
accept_ideas: the debate about what a planet is

if_they_say.when: the student says it is about planets around other stars
if_they_say.ask: Those planets come at the end. What is the part mostly about?

if_they_say.when: the student says it is about how round a planet must be
if_they_say.ask: That is one question astronomers ask. What are they arguing about?

items.prompt: What is this passage mostly about?

tutor_only.confirm: Yes. The word planet means what astronomers agree it means, and that agreement changed when new objects were found.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The parts give the rule, the Pluto case, and the ongoing argument, so the subject is a definition that people make and revise.
tutor_only.tell: The passage is about the definition of planet, and how it changed when new objects were found.
help: Look at what every part is about.
The parts give a rule, a case, and an argument.
tutor_only.core_idea: The definition of planet, and how it changed when new objects were found.
accept_ideas: how the definition of planet was made and changed
what counts as a planet and who decides
the rule that changed Pluto's label

if_they_say.when: the student says it is about Pluto
if_they_say.ask: Pluto is one case. What did it make astronomers do?

if_they_say.when: the student says it is about the solar system
if_they_say.ask: The passage is about one word. Which word?

items.prompt: A reader says the passage is mostly about Pluto. What does that idea miss?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. Pluto is one case that shows why the rule changed, and the passage is about the rule itself.
tutor_only.correct_reason: Pluto appears in the middle as the case that forced the vote, while the first part gives the rule and the last gives the argument.
tutor_only.tell: That idea misses the rule. Pluto is the case that shows why astronomers wrote a new definition.
help: Look at how many parts are about Pluto.
The opening is the rule and the end is the argument.
tutor_only.core_idea: Pluto is the case that shows why the rule changed, and the passage is about the rule.
accept_ideas: it leaves out the three conditions
the passage is about the rule, not one object

if_they_say.when: the student says nothing is missing
if_they_say.ask: Count the parts about Pluto. Then count the parts about the rule and the argument.

if_they_say.when: the student says it leaves out the Moon
if_they_say.ask: The Moon is not in the passage. What is the opening about?
